(Today through Tuesday)...
Issued at 133 AM EDT Wed Aug 12 2026

Overview.

Active weather continues into today with additional rounds of showers 
and thunderstorms. A few storms could produce localized heavy rain 
and strong gusty winds this afternoon and evening with best chances 
across southwest Indiana. A front associated with the system will 
gradually move south into early Thursday with additional marginally 
severe storms through Friday. Rain chances generally look lower for 
the weekend with the jet stream further north into the Great Lakes.

Rest of Tonight.

The main focus through the remainder of the overnight hours will
be additional thunderstorm development across eastern Indiana with
the LLJ ramping up. Storm coverage has been gradually increasing
over the last 2 hours with heavy rain being the main threat along
with occasional pulses leading to small hail. General expectations
are for these storms to grow upscale and move to the southeast
with additional flooding from Madison County south to Decatur
county. With the storms not backbuilding as much as they were
initially, flash flooding should remain isolated with broader
areal flooding being the main threat.

Wednesday Through Thursday.

Indiana remains locked into northwesterly flow with broad ridging 
across the Central Plains and broad troughing across the Great 
Lakes. Shortwaves within the upper level flow will continue to bring 
periods of showers and storms  with upper-level forcing along the 
exit region of a 50-60 kt mid-level jet streak aloft. A weak surface 
front currently across northern Indiana is expected to slowly move 
south through the day but generally will only have minimal impacts 
on storm coverage timing as much of the forcing is being driven by 
the jet level forcing aloft.

WAA and boundary layer heating will yield MLCAPE values ranging 
between 2500-3500 J/kg again today, supported by steep lapse rates 
exceeding 7.5 C/km above the boundary layer. While 0-6 km bulk shear 
vector magnitudes are modest at 25-35 kt, orientation roughly 45 
degrees to the initiating boundary favors mixed mode convective 
structures, including multicellular clusters and bowing segments. 
HREF 2-5 km UH probability sweeps show maximum signal concentrated 
across central and southern Indiana between 21Z and 03Z with storms 
moving in from the west. Elevated DCAPE values above 1000 J/kg 
suggest damaging wind gusts will be the primary severe hazard, with 
steep mid-level lapse rates occasionally supporting isolated severe 
hail. PWATs nearing 1.8 to 2.0 inches, well above the 90th 
percentile, will support efficient warm-rain processes and localized 
torrential rainfall. Ahead of the stronger storms, initiation is 
likely across northern Indiana during the early morning hours today, 
but CAMs continue to struggle with properly diagnosing the current 
boundaries and impacts from the front, so confidence is lower on any 
impacts through the morning hours.

Additional flooding looks likely, especially in areas that saw
heavy rain during the overnight hours. LPMMs show pockets of 2-3
inches beyond what already fell, but confidence is very low in
where this may occur with broader model spread on the location of
the axis of heaviest rain. Thus, will keep the Flood Watch through
04Z and reevaluate later today.

Convection will clear the southern CWA border late tonight as the 
surface cold front gradually drifts into closer to the Ohio River. 
Forecast confidence is fairly low into Thursday with more 
significant model divergence on the broader synoptic pattern and how 
the residual front may impact conditions. North of the front, 
temperatures will be much cooler with highs in the upper 70s to near 
80 with minimal instability, while areas to the south of the front 
are likely to end up near 90. The severe threat generally should be 
on the warmer side with any convection to the north remaining 
elevated.

Friday Through Tuesday.

The broad synoptic regime during the extended period will feature a 
transition from post-frontal surface high pressure to mid-level 
ridge amplification across the Central Mississippi and Ohio Valleys. 
The 00Z GEFS and EPS are in have decent agreement through 00Z 
Monday, with the ridge over the Plains strengthening and pushing the 
jet stream further north into the Great Lakes. Daytime highs will 
climb from the lower 80s on Friday to the upper 80s and low 90s by 
Sunday as return southerly flow returns. Rain chances generally 
should remain limited to just the northern counties, but even that 
looks low.

By Monday into Tuesday, ensemble guidance indicates a northern 
stream trough traversing the Canadian Prairies into the Great Lakes 
region, acting to flatten the mid-level ridge and push a surface 
cold front toward the lower Great Lakes. Guidance exhibits typical
